Removed case, so didn't add a comment
Done

Removed

minor thing, it would most likely be .../system/chassis${chassis}/motherboard.

I don't think it really affects the testcase though.

you'd still want this to be a reference, like
const std::vector<int>&

Code looks good to me.  It wouldn't be merged until there are some commits that use it.  Also, depending on the other files it may be better in a subdir.

General comment on this file. If the data type of a property is not what you are expecting, how is that error handled?  For example, with the code
```
sensor["target_path"].get<std::string>()
```
what happens if the JSON value is an int?

The single chassis json parser file (json_parser.cpp) that I based this off of didn't seem to do a lot of formal type checking, which is why there isn't any here. In the case you mentioned, the `.get` function should throw a `json::type_error`. I added a test for it.

Should this exception message mention fan type or fan definition?

Right now if that exception is caught the message doesn't really indicate what part of the parsing code had a problem.
Changed it to specify that it's missing a fan type definition parameter.
It seems like something is missing here?  Is it supposed to be getting upperDeviation from the JSON file if that property is specified?
Yes, changed it to get the upper_deviation parameter from the JSON if specified.
Should it be checking if the JSON contains these properties?
I added blanket checks for them.

Thank you for doing automated tests.  It is really helpful and important in my opinion.

It would be good to also test the error paths.  For example, when a required property is missing, or a property has an unexpected data type in the JSON.
I added tests that have an unexpected data type (int instead of string) and a missing required property. Those should throw `json::type_error` and `std::runtime_error` exceptions respectively.
Will `json_parser.*` coexist with `multichassis_json_parser.*`?  Or will the multichassis one replace the other?
Per the earlier discussion, I'm assuming the plan is to have them coexist for now, but combine them into a single json parser down the line. Matt might be able to provide more context on that.
What happens when exceptions are thrown due to parsing errors? Does the application core dump, or log an error, or?

I would expect a json error of some sort. For example, there is a test case that checks that a `json::type_error` is thrown if there is a mismatch between the expected type and the actual type in the json.

Is there a reason you used `at()` here instead of `operator[]()`?

`at()` throws if the key doesn't exist. It is not totally clear to me from the docs what `operator[]()` does if the key doesn't exist and the json element is const. I think it is undefined behavior and asserts at runtime.

It doesn't really matter since you are checking on the previous lines if the element contains the key. Just wondering why you picked `at()` here.

This looks like it was carried over from the existing json_parser code. Not sure why the original author used at() over the square bracket operator, since they seem to use the square bracket everywhere else.
Should you validate the chassis numbers? Negative is obviously bad, but 0 may be too?  Chassis 0 represents the entire system vs. an actual chassis (at least on multi-chassis systems).
Talked to Matt about this. He said to run this on a single-chassis system, it would need to accept 0 for a chassis number. I added a check for negative numbers.

There's a lot of common code between the if/else branch. You don't need to change anything now, but if more code gets added to this function later it would probably be worth trying to make most of the code common.
Noted
How is this file going to co-exist in the same repo as types.hpp? Both define SensorDefinition.

They are defined under different namespaces. SensorDefinition in types.hpp is defined under `phosphor::fan::monitor`, and SensorDefinition in this file is under a child namespace(`phosphor::fan::monitor::multi_chassis`).

Thank you for writing automated tests cases. I think they provide tons of value in being able to re-run thousands of times for free after future code modifications. They can also test error conditions that are hard to generate on a real system.
No problem!
Yeah, I think both would probably work in this case. I just did it this way since I used portions from the template to write my test cases.
Is chassis 0 a valid number, since it represents the entire system?

Matt said it does have to accept chassis 0 to work on a single chassis system. I don't think the specific numbers make much of a difference here, though, since this just tests that getZoneDefs creates the right ZoneDefinition struct objects.
